little.can_now: tell a true story of someone who kept going, worked as a team or tried again, and say which skill they used

steps.say: Welcome to the Story Theatre! The buddies act out true stories of real people. You help!
Paris, 1824. Louis Braille could not see. Books for blind children had huge raised letters, slow to feel. Louis, aged 15, made letters of dots instead.
Make Louis's letter B: touch dot 1, then dot 2.
steps.done: B! Blind people read Louis's dots with their fingertips, all over the world.

steps.say: Louis kept working on his dots for years, again and again. Which skill did he use?

choices.why: He didn't give up: he worked on his dots for years.
He didn't wait: he made it himself.

steps.done: Kept going!

steps.say: Kenya, 1977. Wangari Maathai saw trees being cut down and the land getting dry. She started small: with seven trees.
Plant trees with Wangari and her friends: touch each hole.
steps.done: Together, they have planted more than 50 million trees!

steps.say: Wangari didn't plant them alone. Which skill helped most?

choices.why: Nobody could plant millions alone. Many hands did it together.
It wasn't luck: thousands of people worked together.

steps.done: Teamwork!

steps.say: Jamaica and far away, 1854. Mary Seacole asked to go and help sick soldiers. She was told no.
Mary paid for the journey herself and opened a hotel to look after soldiers. Which skill did she use?

choices.text: Kept going and found another way

choices.why: She didn't stop at no: she found another way to help.
She didn't waste time being cross: she found a way.

steps.done: She found another way!

steps.say: America, about 1900. The Wright brothers fixed bicycles, and dreamed of flying. They built gliders.
Launch the glider: touch it.
steps.done: Whoosh... bump. It came down too soon.

steps.say: The glider came down. Which skill did the brothers use?

choices.why: If they had given up, there would be no aeroplanes!
They didn't blame anything: they made better wings.

steps.done: They tried again, and again.

steps.label: 12 seconds
steps.say: 17 December 1903: the first aeroplane flight with an engine! 12 seconds in the air.
Real people built these things step by step. Open the SUCCESS STORIES shelf for twenty true stories!

middle.twist: One more story: Fleming's messy dish.
middle.can_now: tell how real people tested ideas, shared what they knew and used numbers to show the truth

steps.say: Welcome to the Story Theatre! The buddies act out true stories of real people. You help!
America, 1901. Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop and built gliders. Their new glider lifted much less than they hoped.
Test the glider: touch it.
steps.done: Whoosh... bump. Not enough lift.

steps.say: So they built a wind tunnel and tested lots of wing shapes. Test each wing: touch them.
steps.done: Testing small saves trouble big.

steps.label: 12 seconds
steps.say: 17 December 1903: the first aeroplane flight with an engine! 12 seconds, about 37 metres.
Which skill did the Wright brothers use?

choices.why: They didn't wait: they tested and learned.
If they had given up, there would be no aeroplanes.

steps.done: Test, learn, try again!

steps.say: Alabama, USA, about 1900. George Washington Carver taught farmers. Growing cotton every year had made the soil tired and poor.
Help the soil: plant peanuts this year, then cotton next year. Touch the peanut field, then the cotton field.
steps.done: Peanuts put goodness back into the soil, and the cotton grew better.

steps.say: Carver took his lessons to farms on a wagon, a school on wheels. Which skill did he use?

choices.why: He did the opposite: he took his lessons to everyone.
Many couldn't come, so he went to them.

steps.done: Sharing what you know helps everyone.

steps.say: 1854. Florence Nightingale looked after soldiers in a war hospital. It was dirty, and many got ill from germs.
Help Florence's nurses: open the window, fill the basin and change the sheets.
steps.done: A cleaner ward, and fewer soldiers got ill.

steps.say: Florence counted and drew charts, to show that most of the illness could be stopped. Which skill?

choices.text: Using numbers to show the truth

choices.why: Her charts were for something important: showing the truth with numbers.
Her charts did the talking: careful numbers can change minds.

steps.done: Numbers that show the truth can change things.

steps.say: London, 1928. Alexander Fleming finds a messy dish with mould on it. Look closely: touch the dish.
steps.done: Round the mould, the germs have gone!

steps.say: Fleming didn't throw the dish away: he found penicillin. Which skill did he use?

choices.text: Noticing something odd and looking closely

choices.why: If he had tidied it away, nobody would have noticed then.
Surprises can be clues: he looked closely.

steps.done: Noticing: surprises can be clues.

steps.say: Test, share and show the truth: real people succeed like that. Open the SUCCESS STORIES shelf for twenty true stories!

name_it.title: How real people succeed
lines: Test, learn and try again (the Wright brothers).
Share what you know (George Washington Carver).
Let numbers show the truth (Florence Nightingale).
name_it.source: NASA, the Smithsonian, the National Park Service, the Science History Institute and the National Army Museum

middle.try_real: With a grown-up: read or watch one true story of an inventor, and tell your grown-up which skill they used.

sources.fact: Disappointed by their 1901 glider, the Wrights built a wind tunnel to test wing shapes.
sources.source: NASA, the Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics

sources.fact: Carver taught crop rotation with peanuts and sweet potatoes; the Jesup Wagon took lessons to farms from 1906.

big.twist: One more story: Savitribai Phule and her school.
big.can_now: tell how real people helped everyone, checked carefully and kept trying for years, and that failing is part of success

steps.say: Welcome to the Story Theatre! The buddies act out true stories of real people. You help!
Italy, 1859. Henry Dunant, a Swiss businessman, came to a town after a battle. Thousands of wounded soldiers had almost no one to care for them.
Like Henry, ask the town's people to help: touch each one.
steps.done: A whole town helping, soldiers from both sides.

steps.say: He wrote a book, and in 1863 the Red Cross began. Later his business went wrong, but in 1901 he shared the first Nobel Peace Prize. Which skill?

choices.why: There were too many for one person: he got a whole town helping.
He helped everyone, from both sides.

steps.done: Bringing people together, for everyone.

steps.say: USA, 1962. Katherine Johnson did the sums for spaceflights. John Glenn asked her to check the computer's numbers before he flew round the Earth.
Check like Katherine: one lap of the Earth took Glenn about 90 minutes. He flew 3 laps. About how long were the laps?

choices.why: That adds 3 to 90. Each lap is 90 minutes: 3 × 90 = 270.
That's 90 ÷ 3. Three laps is 3 × 90 = 270 minutes.

steps.done: 3 × 90 = 270 minutes: about four and a half hours. Checked!

steps.say: When Katherine said the numbers were right, Glenn was ready to go. Which skill made people trust her?

choices.why: A guess isn't safe for a spaceflight: she checked every step.
Asking good questions was part of her work.

steps.done: Careful checking builds trust.

steps.say: China, the 1960s. Yuan Longping wanted rice plants that gave much more rice, so nobody went hungry. For years he searched the fields.
Search the field like Yuan: find the special plant and touch it.
steps.done: Found it! In 1970 his team found a special wild rice plant, and made rice that gave about a fifth more.

steps.say: Yuan searched for years, and many tries didn't work. Which skill did he use?

choices.why: One try is rarely enough: he searched for years.
He didn't wait: he kept searching.

steps.done: Patience: years of tries.

steps.say: India, 1848. Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls. Some people threw stones and dirt at her on the way. She kept teaching.
It is said she carried a spare sari, changed at school, and taught anyway. Which skill did she use?

choices.why: She didn't fight back: she kept teaching. That took courage.
She didn't give up: the girls needed their teacher.

steps.done: Courage: she kept going for the girls.

steps.say: What do these real stories show about success?

choices.text: People often fail, learn and try again

choices.why: They all had things go wrong. They learned, and went on.
They helped people, taught and found things out: success means many things.

steps.done: Failing is part of the story.

steps.say: Help everyone, check carefully, be patient and keep going. Open the SUCCESS STORIES shelf for twenty true stories!

name_it.title: Success, the real way
lines: Help others, whoever they are (Henry Dunant).
Check carefully, so people can trust you (Katherine Johnson).
Be patient: years of tries (Yuan Longping).
Failing is part of the story: learn, and go on.
name_it.source: The Nobel Prize, NASA, Nature and Britannica

big.try_real: With a grown-up: ask someone you know about a time something went wrong for them, and what they learned and did next.

sources.fact: Dunant organised help for the wounded after Solferino (1859); the ICRC began in 1863; he went bankrupt, and shared the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.
John Glenn asked Katherine Johnson to check the electronic computer's orbit calculations in 1962.
Yuan Longping's team found a male-sterile wild rice in Hainan in 1970; the 1970s hybrids gave about 20-30% more rice.
